clue.text: Sound device for a judge by the finishing line

indicators.note: placed by, i.e. next to, the other piece in the clue's picture

parts.note: the tape is the ribbon stretched across the finishing line of a race
a Recorder is a part-time judge in the English courts

explanation.surface: Someone wants an audio gadget for the official judging a race at the finishing line.
explanation.walkthrough: In England a Recorder is a barrister or solicitor sitting as a part-time judge, so 'a judge' is not the definition but the second half of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine that captures sound on magnetic tape is an audio device.

clue.text: Mosaic part from which sets are made

indicators.note: made means fashioned, so these letters are formed into a new word

explanation.surface: A piece of mosaic, from which whole sets are made.
explanation.definitionFit: A tessera is one of the small tiles or cubes used in mosaic work.

clue.text: Put piano on a vehicle for the dance

parts.note: p is the musical abbreviation for piano, softly
a van is a vehicle

explanation.surface: Load the piano into a van for the dance.
explanation.definitionFit: The pavan is a slow, stately court dance of the sixteenth century.

clue.text: Boxing clever — the wiliness of Alberich ?

definitions.meaning: skill and tactical cunning in the boxing ring
Alberich is the scheming dwarf of Wagner's Ring cycle, so his cunning is craft concerning the Ring

explanation.walkthrough: Alberich is the dwarf who forges the ring in Wagner's opera cycle The Ring of the Nibelung, so his wiles are 'Ring craft'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringcraft is a boxer's tactical skill; the question mark invites reading it as cunning about Wagner's Ring.

clue.text: Seamen sounded cocky

definitions.meaning: made the sound of a cockerel, past tense of crow

explanation.definitionFit: A ship's company is its seamen; a cock crowing in the past tense gives the same word.

clue.text: African prince applied to Siberian monk

parts.note: Ras is an Ethiopian title for a prince or chief
to put in is to apply, as in putting in for a job

explanation.surface: An African prince put in a claim to a Siberian monk.
explanation.walkthrough: RAS is an Ethiopian noble title (as in Ras Tafari).
explanation.definitionFit: Grigori Rasputin was the Siberian mystic monk at the Russian imperial court.

clue.text: Drug-raising — hardhearted priest is in it

indicators.note: hearted means given a heart, so this letter goes into the middle
raising in a down clue lifts the word so it reads upwards, backwards

parts.note: dope is a drug
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: Someone raising drugs is hard-hearted, and a priest is mixed up in it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hardhearted' splits: 'hard' gives H and 'hearted' puts it at the heart of EPOD (DOPE upwards, from 'raising'). The definition describes the vestment a priest is in.
explanation.definitionFit: An ephod is the sleeveless vestment worn by Jewish priests, so a priest is dressed in one.

clue.text: Steering clear of a nullification

parts.note: voiding a contract is nullifying it

explanation.surface: Keeping away from a cancelled agreement.
explanation.definitionFit: Avoiding means keeping away from or evading.

clue.text: One in a team — of musicians possibly

definitions.meaning: a member of a sports side
one of a band or orchestra, someone who performs music

explanation.definitionFit: Both a sports team member and a musician performing an instrument are described by the same word.

clue.text: The main global total ?

parts.note: the main is poetic for the sea, so the main of the whole globe, counted up, is the traditional number of the world's oceans

explanation.walkthrough: 'The main' is an old poetic word for the ocean; the clue asks for the sum of the oceans of the world, as traditionally counted.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase names all the world's oceans, traditionally reckoned as numbering seven.

clue.text: Sussex resort takes money for wretched accommodation

indicators.note: the resort takes on, i.e. adds, the money after itself

parts.note: Hove is a seaside town in Sussex, next to Brighton
L is the abbreviation for pound (librum), a unit of money

explanation.surface: A seaside town pockets cash for providing miserable lodgings.
explanation.walkthrough: Hove is a seaside resort on the English south coast in Sussex; L stands for pounds sterling.
explanation.definitionFit: A hovel is a squalid, miserable little dwelling.

clue.text: Half-blue rejected by nice girl

indicators.note: rejected means thrown back, so the half-word is turned round
half of the word blue is taken, here its second two letters

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A girl who once won a half-blue at university is snubbed by a nice young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half-blue' looks like the Oxbridge sporting award, but it means half of the word 'blue', UE; 'rejected' turns it to EU, then NICE follows.
explanation.definitionFit: Eunice is a female first name.

clue.text: Song of sixpence? Much dearer, we hear, in essence

indicators.note: we hear signals that the phrase built is only said like the answer, not spelt like it

parts.note: a song is a ditty, and a sum much dearer than sixpence is a quid (a pound), so this is a quid ditty

explanation.surface: Someone muses on the nursery rhyme about sixpence, joking it would cost far more now, in essence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sing a Song of Sixpence' is a nursery rhyme; a quid is British slang for a pound, much more than sixpence. QUID DITTY, said aloud, gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Quiddity is a philosophical term for the inherent nature or whatness of a thing.

clue.text: Articles like fruit

parts.note: an is the indefinite article; the plural gives two of them
the second of the two indefinite articles, an again
as means like, as in 'as good as new'

explanation.surface: A list of items resembling fruit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Articles' is plural, so it supplies two copies of AN.
explanation.definitionFit: Ananas is the pineapple, a tropical fruit (its name in French and many other languages).

clue.text: Star in danger going under seat perhaps.

indicators.note: in a down clue the second piece goes under the first
perhaps suggests the word seat in some other possible form, so its letters are rearranged

parts.note: risk is danger

explanation.surface: A celebrity in peril, about to lose their seat perhaps.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star in danger' reads as a celebrity at risk, but 'Star' alone is the definition: 'perhaps' rearranges SEAT to ASTE and RISK goes under it.
explanation.definitionFit: An asterisk is the star-shaped symbol used in print.

clue.text: How promenaders wish to see their mother

definitions.text: How promenaders wish to see their mother

parts.words: How promenaders wish to see their mother
parts.note: at the Last Night of the Proms the audience sing Land of Hope and Glory, which calls Britain the mother of the free and asks that she be made greater yet

explanation.walkthrough: The Proms are London's summer concert season; promenaders stand in the arena. Their anthem Land of Hope and Glory says 'God, who made thee mighty, make thee mightier yet', addressed to the 'Mother of the Free'.
explanation.definitionFit: The song's line wishes the mother country to become more powerful still.

clue.text: Achievement in heraldry — not poultry-farming

definitions.meaning: a diamond-shaped panel bearing a dead person's arms, a funeral achievement
a jokey misreading as the business of hatching chicks, which the clue denies

explanation.walkthrough: In heraldry an 'achievement' is a full display of arms. The second part warns against reading the word as hatching eggs.
explanation.definitionFit: A hatchment is a funeral display of a deceased person's coat of arms, hung outside the house.

clue.text: When Lycidas's swain visits fresh woods

definitions.text: When Lycidas's swain visits fresh woods

parts.words: When Lycidas's swain visits fresh woods
parts.note: Milton's elegy Lycidas ends with the shepherd resolving to go to fresh woods and pastures new on the coming day

explanation.walkthrough: Milton's poem Lycidas closes: 'Tomorrow to fresh woods, and pastures new' (often misquoted as 'fields').
explanation.definitionFit: The poem's last line says the shepherd sets off for new woods on the following day.

clue.text: Prayer. Mexican worker captures bird with one

indicators.note: captures means the worker's letters hold the other pieces inside

parts.note: a peon is a Latin American labourer
a tit is a small songbird
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A prayer is offered as a Mexican labourer catches a bird.
explanation.definitionFit: A petition is a formal request or supplication, as to God.

clue.text: Shepherd in old gold

parts.note: past means old, bygone
or is the heraldic word for gold

explanation.surface: A shepherd dressed in old gold.
explanation.definitionFit: A pastor is a minister who tends a flock, a spiritual shepherd; the word is Latin for herdsman.

clue.text: Way old people travelled by coach

parts.note: St is the abbreviation for street, a way
the aged are old people

explanation.surface: Describing how elderly folk used to get about on coach trips.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is archaic: to 'stage' was to travel by stagecoach.
explanation.definitionFit: To stage once meant to journey by stagecoach, stopping at stages along the route.

clue.text: Granted it could be scraping the bottom

indicators.note: could be means the word granted might become something else, so its letters are reordered

explanation.surface: Granted, it might be scraping the barrel's bottom.
explanation.definitionFit: A drag-net is trawled along the sea or river bed.

clue.text: River's to be diverted by the master's man

indicators.note: a river that is diverted has its course rearranged, so these letters are reordered

parts.note: the word river with its s, read as letters
taken as written

explanation.surface: Plans are made to divert a river, by order of the master's servant.
explanation.definitionFit: A servitor is a male servant or attendant, a master's man.

clue.text: Brand new work by him in 1866

definitions.text: Brand new work by him in 1866

parts.words: Brand new work by him in 1866
parts.note: Brand is a verse play first published in 1866 by the Norwegian dramatist

explanation.walkthrough: 'Brand new' is not 'fresh': Brand is the title of the play, which was new in 1866.
explanation.definitionFit: Henrik Ibsen wrote Brand, published in 1866.

clue.text: One of nine — not all the other things

indicators.note: not all of the word the is used, its last letter being dropped

parts.note: alia is Latin for other things, as in et alia

explanation.surface: One of nine people does not hold with all the rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The nine are the Muses; Thalia is the Muse of comedy. ALIA is Latin for 'other things', familiar from 'et alia'.
explanation.definitionFit: Thalia is one of the nine Muses of Greek myth.

clue.text: Get away, from simple averages

indicators.note: from means the letters are taken out of the run of words simple averages

explanation.surface: Escape, says someone, from boring simple averages.
explanation.definitionFit: To leave is to go away or depart.

clue.text: Young Cratchit was so small

parts.note: the crippled youngest Cratchit boy in Dickens's A Christmas Carol is nicknamed for his small size

explanation.walkthrough: Tiny Tim is the sick little son of Bob Cratchit in Dickens's A Christmas Carol.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective means very small, and is the nickname of Dickens's Tim Cratchit.

clue.text: Desert ship at this watering-place

parts.note: the ship of the desert is the camel, which drinks at a green spot with water in the desert

explanation.walkthrough: 'Desert' is not 'abandon': the 'ship of the desert' is the camel, and this is where it stops to drink.
explanation.definitionFit: An oasis is a fertile place in a desert where water is found.

clue.text: Play hell, having to bring up the firstborn

parts.note: to raise children is to bring them up
Cain was the firstborn son of Adam and Eve

explanation.surface: Bringing up the eldest child can be a nightmare.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise Cain is an idiom meaning to create an uproar or cause trouble.

clue.text: Wherein there's no turning back the wheels of progress

definitions.text: Wherein there's no turning back the wheels of progress

parts.words: Wherein there's no turning back the wheels of progress
parts.note: read literally, a road where vehicle wheels may not turn and come back the other way

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a speech about irreversible progress; literally, it describes a road whose traffic can travel only forward.
explanation.definitionFit: Traffic on such a road may move in one direction only.
